parsed.elsewhere_quote: If all prime factors of \(x\) are at most \(A\), then \(\sigma(x)=P(x)\), which is good by (1). ... Every prime in \(\sigma(b)\) is at most \(A\), whereas every prime in \(P(x)\setminus\sigma(x)\) is greater than \(A\).
parsed.explanation: The counterexample is valid: for A=15 the terms 15,18,20 give sigma(18)={3} under Q={p|A}, which misses P(20), so the Lemma is false under the displayed definition. But the Lemma's proof nowhere uses divisibility of A: it uses 'all prime factors at most A imply sigma(x)=P(x)' and 'every prime in P(x)\sigma(x) is greater than A', both valid only for Q={p prime, p<=A}, and the falsification section names that same set. Section 3 also works verbatim with L the primorial. So the argument for the large-prime erasure is present in full; the definition line (and the gloss 'only the primes dividing A can matter') is a misprint.
